posts.title: An autumn walk to the canal
posts.excerpt: Out of the lattice door, left at the tofu cart, and eight minutes later the willows. The best hour is just after breakfast.
posts.content:
In late October the willows on the canal go yellow from the top down, and the water is so low you can see the stones. Take the bicycles if you want to go further; the path follows the water for three kilometres.

On the way back, the bakery by the bridge sells persimmon bread on Saturdays only. Haru says it is worth the queue.

posts.title: What Haru serves for breakfast
posts.excerpt: Rice from her cousin’s field, miso she makes in March, whatever fish the market had, and pickles from a jar older than the guest book.
posts.content:
Breakfast comes to the door at eight on a lacquered tray. If you would rather sleep, tell Haru the night before and she leaves it at nine instead, with the soup in a flask.

Guests who do not eat fish get tamagoyaki and grilled tofu. Just say so when you book.

posts.title: Planing the hinoki tub
posts.excerpt: Every September the house closes for three days so the carpenter can plane the bath. It comes back pale and smelling of forest.
posts.content:
Hinoki darkens where the water sits. A thin pass with a hand plane takes off half a millimetre and the colour of the wood comes back, along with the smell.

This year he also replaced two boards of the bamboo blind. The new ones will be the same colour as the old by spring.
